reviewer: Codex, source comparison in this editing session
scope: Publisher versions, complete news and opinion articles, and versioned preprint texts for the November 9–15 publication week. Evidence types, original dates and claim locators are identified individually.

checks: The text synthesizes four earlier publications and proposes a design direction; it supplies no new experiment.
Planning, monitoring, feedback and disclosure concerns are attributed to the editorial rather than relabelled as new weekly empirical findings.
Sections 3.1–3.3: 40 undergraduates, ten per cell, 140-second video, ten-item accuracy measure; static AI images versus manually added motion.
Section 4.1 and Table 3: motion main effect on accuracy p=.488, interpreted as no statistically significant evidence, not proof of equivalence.
Sections 4.2 and 5.2: subjective outcomes exploratory, gender observed, multiple comparisons and unmeasured baseline characteristics restrict interpretation.
No delayed independent-learning measure supports a lasting-learning claim.

Results 4.1–4.2. Prior discussion groups were randomized within two classes. The adjusted post-task performance difference was significant with a small descriptive standardized difference. Predicted performance, confidence, bias and absolute error had no statistically detectable between-condition differences.
Assignment at the group level, post-test only, no delayed follow-up.
Table 7 reports links between students’ ratings of AI capability and both reported extraneous cognitive load and academic self-efficacy. Use associative language.

reading_revision_review.reviewer: Separate Codex release review, source comparison
reading_revision_review.source_locator: Publisher HTML, section 4.4, first paragraph and Table 7
reading_revision_review.reason: The automatic digest previously selected the research aim as a result. Its new finding is the actual abstract result: perceived AI capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Independently checked section 4.4 and Table 7, which report coefficients of -0.362 and 0.324 and explicitly describe cross-sectional associations. The selected finding remains labeled abstract-derived; this review does not claim that the missing machine-indexed Results section was recovered.

checks: The 52 papers include 32 added since March. The unit is a paper. Results for studying varied, and offloading could undermine learning.
Five newly added student-facing studies were in US K–12 settings. The November date belongs to the review and not to the primary studies it summarizes.
In the feedback conditions, a model’s history of providing accurate versus inaccurate advice predicted subsequent persuasion. This pattern did not hold without feedback in these tasks.

checks: Reporter interviews designers and educators about an age-based guide. The guide draws on developmental literature. Its proposed mechanisms are not results from thousands of AI trials.
Article separates lawmakers’ November 12 letter about configuring student search from the platform’s account of service-level switches. No student learning or attention outcome was measured.

The anonymous investigator and two named correspondents describe competing perspectives on public access and handling long AI-drafted complaints. The article collects letters and does not estimate prevalence. The earlier November 8 article is outside the window.

Original publication November 10. The November 13 amendment clarifies attribution. Kirman recognizes the benefit of access to tutoring and raises a hypothesis about self-directed judgment without testing an effect.

sources.genre: Randomized comparison of three types of tutoring support
checks: Publisher first-publication date. Authors analyzed 149 students aged 16–18 at one English sixth-form college. In Table 2, second-section perceived difficulty and effort were higher with GenAI than with human tutoring.
Difficulty and effort were self-reports. The study did not measure subsequent learning gains, and its result does not establish a universal tutor effect.

publication_checks: The two existing sources are retained and eleven dated sources are added. The source shelf contains five journal papers, three preprints, one research review, two reported articles, one opinion essay and one collection of letters.
Every source has a claim-level link in a theme or the cross-source discussion. All items are within the November 9–15 UTC source window.
Preserve the November 16 permanent URL, issue number, feed identity and original publication timestamp.
